title: Milestone 3 - Firmware Implementation, FFT/Audio/SD/Wi-Fi & Iterative Hardware Debugging (FRDM-MCXA153)

parts: You are an embedded firmware pair-programmer for a bare-metal MCUXpresso project on the NXP FRDM-MCXA153. Write and modify C in software/source, reason from the MCXA153 reference manual and the actual SDK register headers, and be explicit when a datasheet assumption is unverified so the student can check it on real hardware. AI assists; the human verifies on hardware.

Hardware from Milestone 2 is assembled and verified. Now the firmware. Target: a bare-metal superloop with three user-selectable modes on the three buttons - (1) Synthesizer: play the mic back to the headphones in real time with a selectable voice filter; (2) SD Recorder/Player: record mic audio to WAV on the SD card and play recordings back; (3) Wi-Fi: ESP8266 as a small web server showing status. There's an ILI9341 UI on top. Before writing code, decompose this into clean modules with tight interfaces so I can build and test them one at a time. Keep main.c thin.

Decomposition into four modules, each with a narrow header so you can bring them up independently:

1. audio_engine (audio_engine.c/.h): owns the whole real-time audio path - mic sampling, the FFT, the synth/effects, and audio output. Public surface stays tiny: AudioEngine_Init(), AudioEngine_Process() called once per superloop iteration, AudioEngine_SetMode(), AudioEngine_SetVoiceFilter(), AudioEngine_SetRecordEnable(), AudioEngine_SetPlaybackEnable(). This hides the ADC/timer/output details behind a mode switch.
2. ui_display (ui_display.c/.h): the ILI9341 driver plus screen rendering. ui_display_init(), ui_display_process_loop(), ui_display_mode(mode), and ui_handle_action1/2(mode) so the buttons drive UI actions without the UI knowing about buttons.
3. sdcard_wav (sdcard_wav.c/.h): WAV file record/play on top of FatFS, so the audio engine asks for 'give me/take these samples' and never touches the filesystem directly.
4. wifi_esp (wifi_esp.c/.h): the ESP8266 UART driver and the tiny web server, fed status by the rest of the system.

main.c then reduces to: init clocks/pins/console, init the three buttons (P2_2, P3_13, P3_14) as pull-up inputs, call AudioEngine_Init() and ui_display_init(), then a while(1) that reads/debounces buttons, dispatches to the UI, and calls AudioEngine_Process() and ui_display_process_loop(). That keeps main.c thin and every subsystem independently testable. Shall I scaffold the four module pairs with these signatures?

Scaffolded the four module pairs with the signatures above and reduced main.c to init + superloop dispatch. Each module compiles standalone against stubs, so you can bring them up one at a time. Start with audio_engine so we have something audible/visible to verify against.

Start with the FFT for the spectrum view. The docs I drafted earlier assumed CMSIS-DSP's arm_cfft_f32, but pulling in and configuring the whole CMSIS-DSP pack for a single 256-point transform feels heavy. What's the trade-off, and if hand-rolling is reasonable, implement a small radix-2 FFT in audio_engine.c. Sample rate is 16 kHz, FFT_SIZE 256.

Trade-off: CMSIS-DSP is the right call for large/streaming transforms or when you need vetted numerical accuracy and the M33 DSP extensions squeezed hard. But it means adding the library, a config header, and the twiddle tables to the build, plus float32 buffers. For a single 256-point magnitude spectrum feeding 32 display bars, a hand-rolled radix-2 Cooley-Tukey FFT is only ~40 lines, keeps the build self-contained, and is more than fast enough at 16 kHz because you only transform one 256-sample block per frame, not per sample.

I implemented an in-place radix-2 FFT in audio_engine.c: a bit-reversal permutation, then log2(256)=8 butterfly stages using a small precomputed sin/cos step, operating on real+imag arrays. The mic block is windowed, transformed, then reduced to magnitude sqrt(re^2+im^2) per bin; the lower 128 bins are decimated into 32 spectrum bars with a peak-hold decay for the UI. Accuracy is fine for a visualizer - it's not bit-exact to CMSIS but the peak-bin location is correct, which is what the spectrum needs. Note this diverges from the CMSIS-DSP line in the design doc; I'd update the doc to say 'self-contained radix-2 FFT' so the report matches the code.

I flashed the synth mode and verified on hardware: the mic-to-headphone path makes sound, but it's harsh and noisy - not like clean audio at all. My documentation assumed I was driving a real DAC on P3_12 (DAC_OUT). Before I chase this as a filter/gain bug, can you confirm from the actual MCXA153 register headers whether this chip even HAS a general-purpose audio DAC peripheral? I don't want to keep debugging against a wrong assumption.

You were right to stop and check the assumption - this is the root cause, not a gain bug. Checking the MCXA153's own SDK register headers: there is NO general-purpose audio DAC peripheral on this part. The only on-chip 'DAC-like' block is an internal comparator reference (a DAC used as a threshold for the analog comparator), which cannot drive an external audio load. So 'DAC_OUT on P3_12' in the design doc was an incorrect assumption carried over from a different MCU family.

That completely explains the harsh sound: to get audio out at all, the firmware was effectively toggling P3_12 as a 1-bit output, and a raw 1-bit stream is full of high-frequency quantization noise - it will sound gritty no matter how you set the gain.

The correct approach on a DAC-less MCU is a delta-sigma (sigma-delta) modulator in software: oversample far above the audio band and push the quantization noise up out of the audible range so a simple analog filter can remove it. I replaced the naive 1-bit output with a 2nd-order noise-shaped delta-sigma modulator on P3_12 running around ~192 kHz. Second order shapes the noise more steeply than first order, so after filtering the audible band is much cleaner. This is a firmware fix, but it only sounds good with the analog fix in the next step - the doc should be corrected to 'no hardware DAC; 1-bit delta-sigma bitstream on P3_12.'

That makes sense - a 1-bit stream straight into the jack is why it sounded bad. So the 1k series resistor alone isn't enough; I need to actually low-pass that bitstream in analog. Give me the RC values to reconstruct audio from a ~192 kHz delta-sigma stream, and on the firmware side improve the mic front-end too - it's quiet and noisy. Add automatic gain and some anti-alias smoothing on the input.

Analog reconstruction filter (the missing piece):
- You already have ~1k in series with P3_12. Add a capacitor to GND after it to form an RC low-pass. Target a cutoff above the audio band (~20 kHz) but far below the 192 kHz carrier so the delta-sigma noise is removed. With R=1k, C=15nF gives fc = 1/(2*pi*R*C) ~ 10.6 kHz; C=10nF gives ~15.9 kHz. Use ~15-22nF to GND. That single RC turns the bitstream back into a smooth analog waveform - it is the difference between 'grinding noise' and 'music.' A second RC stage cleans it further if you want.

Firmware mic front-end improvements (done in audio_engine.c):
- Remove DC bias: subtract the ~1.65V (mid-scale) offset so the sample is centered on zero before processing.
- AGC: track a running envelope of the input and scale toward a target level, with fast attack / slow release, so quiet speech is boosted without pumping on loud sounds.
- Anti-alias / smoothing: a light 1st-order IIR low-pass on the input path to knock down out-of-band content and hiss before it hits the FFT and the output modulator.
- These feed the same 2nd-order noise-shaped output, so with the RC filter in place the synth path should sound clean. Re-test on hardware and adjust the AGC target and RC cutoff by ear.

Now mode 2, the SD recorder. Implement WAV record and playback on FatFS. Important constraint: the SD card shares the SPI pins with the ILI9341 (SCK P2_12 / MOSI P2_13, plus MISO P2_16 and its own CS P1_3). I don't want to disturb the hand-rolled LCD driver that already works. Also my wiring has no card-detect pin - how do we know a card is present?

To avoid disturbing the working LCD driver, I implemented the SD access as bit-banged SPI on the same SCK/MOSI pins the LCD already uses, adding MISO on P2_16 and the SD's own CS on P1_3. Bit-banging here is a deliberate simplification: the LCD driver is hand-rolled and stable, and sharing the LPSPI0 hardware peripheral between them would mean re-plumbing that driver's timing and CS handling. Bit-banging the SD keeps the two paths fully independent - only the CS discipline (assert SD_CS, transact, deassert; never overlap with the LCD CS) couples them, which is exactly the R-001 risk we flagged in Milestone 2. FatFS's diskio layer sits on top of this bit-banged SPI.

WAV: on record, write a standard 44-byte RIFF/WAV header (PCM, mono, 16-bit, 16 kHz), then stream raw PCM samples, flushing periodically so a yanked card loses at most a small tail; on stop, seek back and patch the header's length fields. Playback parses that header and feeds samples to the audio output path.

Card-detect: since your wiring has no CD pin, there is no electrical 'card present' signal. The robust substitute is to treat the result of f_mount()/card init as presence: if mounting succeeds, a card is in; if it fails, report 'no card.' I made the SD Recorder screen re-attempt the mount each time it is opened, so inserting a card and reopening the screen picks it up without a reboot.

Mode 3: the ESP8266 web server on LPUART2 (P1_4 RX / P1_5 TX). Bring up the UART, talk to the module with AT commands, and serve a small status page. One thing I'm not sure about and can't fully verify without the board in front of me: the exact pin-mux ALT function index for those two pins. Be explicit about what's confirmed vs. what I need to check on hardware.

Implemented wifi_esp.c: init LPUART2 at 115200 8N1, then an AT sequence - AT (probe), AT+CWMODE, AT+CWJAP/or SoftAP, AT+CIPMUX=1, AT+CIPSERVER=1 to open a listening socket - and a minimal HTTP responder that answers a GET with a small status page (mode, sample rate, SD present, uptime) via AT+CIPSEND. It is fed status by the rest of the system so the page reflects live state.

Confirmed vs. needs-hardware-check, being explicit as you asked:
- CONFIRMED from the SDK: LPUART2 exists and 115200 8N1 is a standard config; the AT command flow is per the ESP8266 AT firmware.
- NEEDS A HARDWARE CHECK: the exact pin-mux ALT index for P1_4 and P1_5 to route LPUART2_RXD/TXD. My best reading of the MCXA153 pin-signal multiplexing table is ALT4 on P1_4 (LPUART2_RXD) and ALT3 on P1_5 (LPUART2_TXD), but I could not confirm this against a working link. If the ESP8266 does not answer 'AT' with 'OK', the first thing to re-check is these ALT values in the MCUXpresso Config Tool / reference manual - a wrong ALT means the UART signal never reaches the pin even though the code is correct. Also verify TX/RX are crossed (MCU TX -> ESP RX) and EN is tied high.

Let's close out the milestone. Do a full clean build of the whole firmware and confirm it links. Then summarize what I should carry into my documentation - specifically the three places where the real hardware forced the firmware to diverge from my original design assumptions, because those are the engineering lessons I want to write up and the hardware follow-ups I still owe.

Clean build: the full firmware (audio_engine, ui_display, sdcard_wav, wifi_esp, FatFS, SDK drivers) compiles and links to the target ELF with no errors - all four modules integrate under the thin main.c superloop.

The three places real hardware forced a divergence from the original design - your write-up lessons and the follow-ups you still owe:
1. No hardware audio DAC. The design assumed a DAC on P3_12; the MCXA153 register headers show no general-purpose audio DAC (only a comparator reference). Firmware output is therefore a 2nd-order noise-shaped 1-bit delta-sigma bitstream on P3_12. Lesson: verify a peripheral exists in the actual part's headers before designing around it. Follow-up you owe: fit the analog RC reconstruction low-pass (~1k series already present + ~15-22nF to GND) on the jack line and judge audio quality with that in place.
2. SD card is bit-banged SPI, not LPSPI0 hardware. Chosen to avoid disturbing the working hand-rolled LCD driver; it shares the LCD's SCK/MOSI and adds MISO (P2_16) + SD_CS (P1_3). Lesson: isolating a risky change from working code can be worth a 'less elegant' implementation. Follow-up: exercise SD + display together and confirm CS lines never overlap (the R-001 shared-bus risk).
3. No card-detect and unverified ESP UART pin-mux. Card presence is inferred from f_mount() success (re-tried when the SD screen opens); the LPUART2 ALT indices for P1_4/P1_5 (best reading: ALT4/ALT3) are unconfirmed. Lesson: make unverifiable assumptions explicit rather than hiding them. Follow-up: confirm those ALT values on the board if the ESP8266 doesn't respond to AT.
All three are already noted as caveats; put them in the documentation's implementation-notes section so the report matches the code that actually runs.
